The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), as used to form the time-oriented Lorentzian geometric data below. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a Hausdorff, second-countable, oriented and time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold without boundary, with signature $(-,+,+,+)$, and assume it is globally hyperbolic in the convention of [[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]]: strongly causal and with compact causal diamonds. Curves and the causal sets $J^\pm(K)$ use the locally absolutely continuous causal-curve convention of [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]].

Write the positive metric density in a chart as $\mu_g=|\det(g_{ab})|^{1/2}|dx^0dx^1dx^2dx^3|$. This is a coordinate-independent smooth density: if $y=\psi(x)$, then $g_y=(D\psi^{-1})^Tg_xD\psi^{-1}$, so $|\det(g_y)|^{1/2}=|\det D\psi^{-1}|\,|\det(g_x)|^{1/2}$, the test-density transformation rule of [[def-qftx-distributions-on-smooth-manifolds]]. Let $\mathcal D_g(M):=C_c^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ have the real test-function topology transported by $f\mapsto f\mu_g$ from that supplier's compactly supported smooth test densities. Give $C^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ its usual topology of uniform convergence of every coordinate derivative on each compact subset.

For a real $V\in C^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ define the scalar Klein–Gordon-type operator $P=-\Box_g+V$, where $\Box_g f:=\mu_g^{-1}\partial_a(\mu_g g^{ab}\partial_b f)$ in a chart. Its principal symbol is $-g^{ab}\xi_a\xi_b$. No physical units are assigned; this is a mathematical differential operator. The Green-data interface below requires formal self-adjointness with respect to $\mu_g$, meaning $\int_M f(Pu)\,\mu_g=\int_M (Pf)u\,\mu_g$ for every $f\in\mathcal D_g(M)$ and $u\in C^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$; these integrals are finite because $P$ is local. The real solution space with spacelike-compact support is

$$\operatorname{Sol}_{\mathrm{sc}}(M):=\{u\in C^\infty(M;\mathbb R): Pu=0\text{ and }\operatorname{supp}u\subseteq J^+(K)\cup J^-(K)\text{ for some compact }K\subset M\}.$$

A **Green-data interface** for $(M,g,N,P)$ consists of continuous real-linear maps $E_+,E_-:\mathcal D_g(M)\to C^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$, called respectively retarded and advanced Green maps, such that for each $f\in\mathcal D_g(M)$,

$$PE_+f=E_+Pf=f,\qquad PE_-f=E_-Pf=f,$$

$$\operatorname{supp}(E_+f)\subseteq J^+(\operatorname{supp}f),\qquad \operatorname{supp}(E_-f)\subseteq J^-(\operatorname{supp}f).$$

The interface also includes uniqueness of the smooth Cauchy problem for $P$. For a smooth spacelike Cauchy hypersurface $\Sigma$ as defined in [[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]], let $\nu$ denote its unique future-directed unit timelike normal, characterized by orthogonality to $T\Sigma$, $g(\nu,\nu)=-1$ and $g(\nu,N)<0$; the Cauchy data of a smooth $u$ are $u|_\Sigma$ and the normal derivative $\nu(u)|_\Sigma$. The uniqueness condition is that a smooth solution of $Pu=0$ with both data zero on $\Sigma$ is zero.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(M,g,N)$ have the geometric hypotheses of the Green-data definition. If $K,L\subseteq M$ are compact and $A,B\subseteq M$ are closed with $A\subseteq J^+(K)$ and $B\subseteq J^-(L)$, then $A\cap B$ is compact. More generally every closed subset of $J^+(K)\cap J^-(L)$ is compact. This assertion requires no Green maps and does not assume that $J^\pm(K)$ themselves are closed.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, let $K\subseteq M$ be compact, and let $W\subseteq M$ be open with $K\subseteq W$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:M\to [0,1]$ that equals $1$ on an open neighbourhood of $K$ and satisfies $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq W$.

derivations.claim: Since $PE_+f=PE_-f=f$, $P(Ef)=0$. Its support is contained in $J^+(\operatorname{supp}f)\cup J^-(\operatorname{supp}f)$ by [F1], so $Ef\in\operatorname{Sol}_{\mathrm{sc}}(M)$. Also $E(Pf)=E_-Pf-E_+Pf=f-f=0$. Hence $P\mathcal D_g(M)\subseteq\ker E$.

Let $f,h\in\mathcal D_g(M)$, $u=E_-f$ and $v=E_+h$. Their supports meet in the closed set $C:=\operatorname{supp}u\cap\operatorname{supp}v$, contained in $J^-(\operatorname{supp}f)\cap J^+(\operatorname{supp}h)$ and compact by [F2]. If $C=\varnothing$, both $fv$ and $uh$ vanish; otherwise choose by [F3] a compactly supported smooth cutoff $\eta$ equal to $1$ on a neighborhood of $C$. Since $f=Pu$ and $h=Pv$, formal self-adjointness applied to the compactly supported functions $\eta u$ and $\eta v$ gives $\int_M f v\,\mu_g=\int_M u h\,\mu_g$: after expanding $P(\eta u)$ and $P(\eta v)$, each commutator term is supported where a derivative of $\eta$ meets $\operatorname{supp}u\cap\operatorname{supp}v\subseteq C$, so it vanishes because $\eta=1$ near $C$; the remaining integrands $fv$ and $uh$ are supported in $C$. Applying the same calculation with $u=E_+f$ and $v=E_-h$ gives $\int_M f(E_-h)\,\mu_g=\int_M (E_+f)h\,\mu_g$. Subtracting these two Green adjoint identities yields $E^*=-E$ under the compact test-density pairing.

Conversely suppose $Ef=0$, so $u:=E_-f=E_+f$. Then $Pu=f$ by [F1] and $\operatorname{supp}u\subseteq J^-(K)\cap J^+(K)$, where $K=\operatorname{supp}f$ is compact. Its closed support is compact by [F2], so the smooth function $u$ is compactly supported. Thus $u\in\mathcal D_g(M)$ and $f=Pu\in P\mathcal D_g(M)$. Together with step 1.1, $\ker E=P\mathcal D_g(M)$.

If $f$ is replaced by $f+Pk$, then $\int_M(Pk)(Eh)\,\mu_g=\int_M kP(Eh)\,\mu_g=0$ by the formal adjoint identity in [F1] and step 1.1; if $h$ is replaced by $h+Pk$, then $E(Pk)=0$ by step 1.1. Thus $\sigma_M$ is well-defined on $V(M)$. Bilinearity follows from linearity of $E$ and the integral. From step 1.2, $\sigma_M([h],[f])=\int hEf\,\mu_g=-\int fEh\,\mu_g=-\sigma_M([f],[h])$, so it is alternating. If $\sigma_M([f],[h])=0$ for every $[h]$, step 1.2 gives $\int_M (Ef)h\,\mu_g=0$ for every compact smooth real $h$. If $Ef$ were nonzero at a point, continuity would give a relatively compact coordinate neighborhood on which it has one strict sign; choose a smaller compact coordinate ball there and use [F3] to obtain a nonnegative test bump equal to $1$ on that ball. Its integral against $Ef\mu_g$ is then nonzero because $\mu_g$ is a positive smooth density and the ball has positive volume, a contradiction. Hence $Ef=0$, and step 2.1 gives $[f]=0$. This proves nondegeneracy and completes the proof.

derivations.claim: First the displayed Weyl relations define an associative unital $*$-algebra on the finite formal sums. For $v,w,z\in V(M)$, the exponent in $(W(v)W(w))W(z)$ is $-\tfrac i2(\sigma(v,w)+\sigma(v+w,z))$, whereas the exponent in $W(v)(W(w)W(z))$ is $-\tfrac i2(\sigma(w,z)+\sigma(v,w+z))$; bilinearity makes these equal. Also $W(0)W(v)=W(v)=W(v)W(0)$ since $\sigma(0,v)=\sigma(v,0)=0$, and $W(v)W(-v)=W(0)$ since $\sigma(v,-v)=0$. The involution reverses products because alternation gives $\sigma(w,v)=-\sigma(v,w)$; hence the relations are consistent with the claimed unit and involution.

Put $S_\iota[f]:=[\iota_*f]$. It is well-defined because $\iota_*(P_U k)=P_M(\iota_*k)$ by [F4], so changing $f$ by an element of $P_U\mathcal D_g(U)$ changes $\iota_*f$ by an element of $P_M\mathcal D_g(M)$. For $f\in\mathcal D_g(U)$, the restriction $u=(E_M^\pm\iota_*f)|_U$ solves $P_Uu=f$. Its support lies in $J_M^\pm(\operatorname{supp}f)\cap U=J_U^\pm(\operatorname{supp}f)$: the inclusion from right to left is immediate, and the reverse follows because a causal curve in $M$ from a point of $\operatorname{supp}f\subset U$ to a point of $U$ remains in $U$ by causal convexity [F4]. Here is the uniqueness argument actually needed. If $w$ is the difference of $u$ and $E_U^+f$, then $P_Uw=0$ and $\operatorname{supp}w\subseteq J_U^+(\operatorname{supp}f)$. For any compact smooth real $h$ on $U$, set $v=E_U^-h$. The closed overlap of their supports is compact by [F5]. A compact cutoff $\eta=1$ near that overlap from [F6] gives $\int_U wh\,\mu_g=\int_U wPv\,\mu_g=\int_U(Pw)v\,\mu_g=0$: apply formal self-adjointness first to $\eta w$ and $v$; every commutator term has a derivative of $\eta$ where both supports meet and hence vanishes. A smooth nonzero real $w$ has a small fixed-sign coordinate neighborhood and a nonnegative test bump there, contradicting this vanishing integral. Thus $w=0$. The advanced case interchanges the signs. Hence $u=E_U^\pm f$ without presupposing uniqueness in the definition. The isometry preserves $\mu_g$, so this compatibility gives $\sigma_M(S_\iota[f],S_\iota[h])=\int_U f(E_Uh)\,\mu_{g_U}=\sigma_U([f],[h])$; thus $S_\iota$ is symplectic.

Define $\alpha_\iota$ on each basis symbol by $\alpha_{\iota}\bigl(W_U(v)\bigr)=W_M(S_\iota v)$ and extend complex-linearly to finite sums. Since $S_\iota$ is symplectic, applying $\alpha_\iota$ to the product in [F3] gives $e^{-i\sigma_U(v,w)/2}W_M(S_{\iota}(v+w))=W_M(S_\iota v)W_M(S_\iota w)$; applying it to $W_U(v)^*$ gives $W_M(-S_\iota v)=W_M(S_\iota v)^*$. It also sends $W_U(0)$ to $W_M(0)$, so it is a unital $*$-homomorphism. If $f$ is supported in an open $O\subseteq U$, then $\iota_*f$ is supported in $\operatorname{im}(\iota|_O)$; therefore the generator formula sends each local generator into $\mathfrak W_M(\operatorname{im}(\iota|_O))$, and sums and products do too. Extension by zero respects identity and composition, hence the generator formula gives $\alpha_{\mathrm{id}}=\mathrm{id}$ and $\alpha_{\jmath\circ\iota}=\alpha_\jmath\circ\alpha_\iota$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]) for the curve calculus and auxiliary-length suppliers. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a globally hyperbolic
time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]] clause (c)) and let

chart-Lebesgue-null Borel set. Let $L:=\ln$ denote the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]]) and define the **volume time function**
$$t:M\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad t(p):=L\bigl(\mu(I^-(p))\bigr)-L\bigl(\mu(I^+(p))\bigr) =\ln\frac{\mu(I^-(p))}{\mu(I^+(p))}.$$
Then:

**(a)** $t$ is well defined and continuous on $M$;

**(b)** $t$ is strictly increasing along causal relations: if $p\le q$
with $p\ne q$, then $t(p)<t(q)$; in particular $t$ is a time function in
the sense of [[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]] clause
(d);

**(c)** for every inextendible future-directed causal curve
$\gamma:I\to M$ one has
$$\lim_{s\to\sup I}t(\gamma(s))=+\infty,\qquad \lim_{s\to\inf I}t(\gamma(s))=-\infty;$$

**(d)** every level set $t^{-1}(c)$, $c\in\mathbb R$, is a Cauchy set
([[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]] clause (c)); in
particular it is acausal, and it is met in exactly one parameter value by
every inextendible causal curve.

No smoothness of $t$ is asserted.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]],
[[def-dependent-choice]]) for the absolutely continuous causal-curve
calculus and the supplied causal results used below.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $S\subseteq M$ be a Cauchy set
([[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]] clause (c)): every
inextendible causal curve $\gamma:I\to M$ has
$\gamma^{-1}[S]=\{t\in I:\gamma(t)\in S\}$ of exactly one element. Then:

**(a)** there is no nonconstant future causal curve $\delta:[a,b]\to M$
with $\delta(a)=\delta(b)$; in particular $S$ is achronal and acausal, and
the three sets $I^-(S)$, $S$, $I^+(S)$ are pairwise disjoint with
$$M=I^-(S)\;\sqcup\;S\;\sqcup\;I^+(S);$$
moreover for $x\notin S$ one has $x\in I^+(S)$ if and only if some point of
$S$ chronologically precedes $x$;

**(b)** $S$ is closed in $M$;

**(c)** for every $p\in S$ there are a chart $(U,x)$ of the kind produced by
[[lem-gr-dominating-cone-bounds]] clauses (a) and (d) around $p$, with
$x(p)=0$ and the supplier constants $K\ge1$ and $c=16$, and numbers $a,\rho,\eta>0$ with $\sqrt c\,\rho+\eta<a$ and
$W:=x^{-1}\bigl((-a,a)\times B_\rho(0)\bigr)\subseteq U$ such that for every
$z\in B_\rho(0)$ the coordinate vertical line
$L_z=x^{-1}\bigl((-a,a)\times\{z\}\bigr)$ meets $S\cap W$ in exactly one
point $x^{-1}(\varphi(z),z)$, and
$$|\varphi(z)-\varphi(z')|\le\sqrt c\,|z-z'|\qquad(z,z'\in B_\rho(0)),$$
with $\varphi(0)=0$ and $|\varphi(z)|\le\sqrt c\,|z|<a$. The cylinder $W$ may be chosen inside any prescribed neighborhood of $p$. Consequently the maps
$z\mapsto x^{-1}(\varphi(z),z)$ form a topological atlas on the closed set
$S$, making $S$ a topological $3$-manifold in the subspace topology whose
inclusion into $M$ is a topological embedding.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $(M,g,N)$ be a
time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold that is globally hyperbolic in
the sense of [[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]] clause
(c): strongly causal and with compact causal diamonds
$J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)$ for all $p,q\in M$. Let $h$ be the auxiliary metric of
[[thm-gr-auxiliary-complete-riemannian-metric]] and let $\le$, $J^\pm$ be the
relations of [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]]. Then:

**(a)** the causal relation is closed: if $p_k\le q_k$ for all $k$ and
$p_k\to p$, $q_k\to q$, then $p\le q$; consequently $J^+(x)$ and $J^-(x)$
are closed for every $x$, and so are $J^+(K)$ and $J^-(K)$ for every compact
$K\subseteq M$;

**(b)** for all compact $K_1,K_2\subseteq M$ the set
$J^+(K_1)\cap J^-(K_2)$ is compact.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $(M,g,N)$ be a
globally hyperbolic time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]] clause (c)), let
$t$ be the volume time function of [[thm-gr-volume-time-function]] and for
$b\in\mathbb R$ let $S_b:=t^{-1}(b)$, a Cauchy set. Then for every compact
$K\subseteq M$ the set
$$J^+(K)\cap J^-(S_b)$$
is compact; moreover
$$J^-(S_b)=\{q\in M:t(q)\le b\},\qquad J^+(S_a)=\{q\in M:t(q)\ge a\}.$$
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every open cover of a smooth manifold admits a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]],
[[def-dependent-choice]]) for the absolutely continuous causal-curve
calculus and the supplied causal results used below.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold, with the
relations $\ll$, $\le$ and the sets $I^\pm$, $J^\pm$ of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] and the future and past sets of
[[def-gr-future-and-past-sets]]. Then:

**(a) Openness.** For every $x\in M$ the chronological future $I^+(x)$ and
the chronological past $I^-(x)$ are open subsets of $M$.

**(b) The chronological relation is open.** The set
$$\{(x,y)\in M\times M:\ x\ll y\}$$
is open in the product topology of $M\times M$.

**(c) Closure of future and past sets.** Let $F\subseteq M$ be a future set,
that is $I^+(F)\subseteq F$. Then every $q\in\overline F$ satisfies
$I^+(q)\subseteq F$. Dually, if $P$ is a past set ($I^-(P)\subseteq P$) and
$q\in\overline P$, then $I^-(q)\subseteq P$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), and let causal
curves be those of [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]].

**(a) Convergent ends are extendible.** Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]) for the general absolutely continuous endpoint argument in this clause. Let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a future
causal curve and suppose $b:=\sup I<\infty$ and $\gamma(t)\to x\in M$ as
$t\to\sup I$. Then there is $\varepsilon>0$ and a future causal curve
$\tilde\gamma$ defined on $I\cup[b,b+\varepsilon)$ whose restriction to $I$
is $\gamma$. Consequently a future-inextendible causal curve whose domain is
bounded above does not converge at its upper end, and the dual statement
holds at the past end.

**(b) Maximal geodesics have no limit.** Let $(p,v)\in TM$ with $v\ne0$ and
let $\gamma_{p,v}:I_{p,v}\to M$ be the unique maximal geodesic with
$\gamma_{p,v}(0)=p$ and $\gamma_{p,v}'(0)=v$, as supplied by
[[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]] clause (a). Then
$\gamma_{p,v}(t)$ does not converge to any point of $M$ as $t\to\sup I_{p,v}$
or as $t\to\inf I_{p,v}$ (where convergence at an infinite end means
convergence as $t\to+\infty$ or $t\to-\infty$ respectively).

**(c) Segments lie on inextendible causal curves.** Let $\gamma:[t_0,t_1]\to M$
with $t_0<t_1$ be a future causal curve, or a past causal curve. Then there
is an inextendible causal curve $\hat\gamma:J\to M$ (same direction as
$\gamma$ in the case at hand) and a strictly increasing affine map
$\rho:[t_0,t_1]\to J$ with $\hat\gamma\circ\rho=\gamma$. In particular, any
two distinct points $p,q\in M$ with $p\le q$ and $p\ne q$ lie on a common
inextendible causal curve, and likewise for the past relation.

**(d) Cauchy sets are acausal.** Every Cauchy set of
[[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]] clause (c) is acausal in
the sense of clause (b) of that definition.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$\nabla$ be its metric-selected connection, whose existence and uniqueness are
supplied by [[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]; its
Christoffel symbols are the smooth chart functions of
[[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]. Recall that a **geodesic**
is a curve with $D_t\gamma'=0$ in its parameter
([[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]],
[[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]).

**(a) Local existence, uniqueness and maximality.** For every $(p,v)\in TM$
there is a unique maximal geodesic $\gamma_{p,v}:I_{p,v}\to M$ with
$\gamma_{p,v}(0)=p$ and $\gamma_{p,v}'(0)=v$; its domain $I_{p,v}$ is an open
interval containing $0$ and is not asserted to be all of $\mathbb R$.

**(b) Smooth dependence.** The set
$\mathcal G:=\{(t,p,v):t\in I_{p,v}\}\subseteq\mathbb R\times TM$ is open, and
the evaluation map $(t,p,v)\mapsto\gamma_{p,v}(t)$ is smooth on $\mathcal G$.

**(c) Scaling.** For every $s\in\mathbb R$ and every $t\in\mathbb R$,
$t\in I_{p,sv}$ if and only if $st\in I_{p,v}$, and then
$\gamma_{p,sv}(t)=\gamma_{p,v}(st)$.

**(d) The exponential map.** Define $\mathcal E_p:=\{v\in T_pM:1\in I_{p,v}\}$
and $\exp_p:\mathcal E_p\to M$, $\exp_p(v):=\gamma_{p,v}(1)$, and let
$\psi_p:T_pM\to\mathbb R^4$ be the coordinate isomorphism of a basis
$e_0,\dots,e_3$ of $T_pM$. Then $\mathcal E_p$ is open and star-shaped about
$0$ (if $v\in\mathcal E_p$ and $0\le s\le1$, then $sv\in\mathcal E_p$),
$\exp_p$ is smooth, $\exp_p(0)=p$, and, under the canonical identification
$T_0(T_pM)\cong T_pM$ induced by the chart $\psi_p$ on $T_pM$,
$$d(\exp_p)_0=\operatorname{id}_{T_pM}.$$
Consequently there is a star-shaped open neighborhood $W_p\subseteq\mathcal E_p$
of $0$ such that $\exp_p|_{W_p}$ is a diffeomorphism onto an open subset of
$M$.

For a Green-data background of [[def-qftx-green-hyperbolic-interface]], let $(V(M),\sigma_M)$ be the real symplectic vector space of [[lem-qftx-green-propagator-symplectic-quotient]]. Define its **algebraic Weyl $*$-algebra** $\mathfrak W(M)$ to be the complex vector space of finite formal sums of basis symbols $W_M(v)$, $v\in V(M)$, with bilinear product and conjugate-linear involution specified on generators by

$$W_M(v)W_M(w):=e^{-i\sigma_M(v,w)/2}W_M(v+w),\qquad W_M(v)^*:=W_M(-v).$$

The unit is $W_M(0)$. This is the algebraic Weyl algebra: this definition assigns no norm, Hilbert-space representation, or $C^*$-completion. For an open set $O\subseteq M$, define the local algebra $\mathfrak W_M(O)$ as the unital $*$-subalgebra generated by the symbols $W_M([f])$ with real $f\in\mathcal D_g(M)$ and $\operatorname{supp}f\subseteq O$. No norm closure is taken.

An **admissible Green-background morphism** $\iota:(U,g_U,N_U,P_U,E^U_+,E^U_-)\to(M,g_M,N_M,P_M,E^M_+,E^M_-)$ is an orientation-preserving, time-orientation-preserving isometric smooth embedding with open causally convex image, for which $P_M\iota_*f=\iota_*P_Uf$ on compact smooth real tests. Here $\iota_*f$ is extension by zero from the open image, which is smooth and compactly supported because $\operatorname{supp}f$ is compact in $U$. The morphism is **Cauchy** when its image contains a Cauchy hypersurface of $(M,g_M,N_M)$, meaning a spacelike embedded hypersurface met exactly once by every inextendible causal curve, as in [[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]]. The associated quotient map, when well-defined, sends $[f]\in V(U)$ to $[\iota_*f]\in V(M)$, and the Weyl map is required to send $W_U([f])$ to $W_M([\iota_*f])$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), as used to form the time-oriented Lorentzian geometric data below. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a Hausdorff, second-countable, oriented and time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold without boundary, with signature $(-,+,+,+)$, and assume it is globally hyperbolic in the convention of [[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]]: strongly causal and with compact causal diamonds. Curves and the causal sets $J^\pm(K)$ use the locally absolutely continuous causal-curve convention of [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]].

Write the positive metric density in a chart as $\mu_g=|\det(g_{ab})|^{1/2}|dx^0dx^1dx^2dx^3|$. This is a coordinate-independent smooth density: if $y=\psi(x)$, then $g_y=(D\psi^{-1})^Tg_xD\psi^{-1}$, so $|\det(g_y)|^{1/2}=|\det D\psi^{-1}|\,|\det(g_x)|^{1/2}$, the test-density transformation rule of [[def-qftx-distributions-on-smooth-manifolds]]. Let $\mathcal D_g(M):=C_c^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ have the real test-function topology transported by $f\mapsto f\mu_g$ from that supplier's compactly supported smooth test densities. Give $C^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ its usual topology of uniform convergence of every coordinate derivative on each compact subset.

For a real $V\in C^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ define the scalar Klein–Gordon-type operator $P=-\Box_g+V$, where $\Box_g f:=\mu_g^{-1}\partial_a(\mu_g g^{ab}\partial_b f)$ in a chart. Its principal symbol is $-g^{ab}\xi_a\xi_b$. No physical units are assigned; this is a mathematical differential operator. The Green-data interface below requires formal self-adjointness with respect to $\mu_g$, meaning $\int_M f(Pu)\,\mu_g=\int_M (Pf)u\,\mu_g$ for every $f\in\mathcal D_g(M)$ and $u\in C^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$; these integrals are finite because $P$ is local. The real solution space with spacelike-compact support is

$$\operatorname{Sol}_{\mathrm{sc}}(M):=\{u\in C^\infty(M;\mathbb R): Pu=0\text{ and }\operatorname{supp}u\subseteq J^+(K)\cup J^-(K)\text{ for some compact }K\subset M\}.$$

A **Green-data interface** for $(M,g,N,P)$ consists of continuous real-linear maps $E_+,E_-:\mathcal D_g(M)\to C^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$, called respectively retarded and advanced Green maps, such that for each $f\in\mathcal D_g(M)$,

$$PE_+f=E_+Pf=f,\qquad PE_-f=E_-Pf=f,$$

$$\operatorname{supp}(E_+f)\subseteq J^+(\operatorname{supp}f),\qquad \operatorname{supp}(E_-f)\subseteq J^-(\operatorname{supp}f).$$

The interface also includes uniqueness of the smooth Cauchy problem for $P$. For a smooth spacelike Cauchy hypersurface $\Sigma$ as defined in [[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]], let $\nu$ denote its unique future-directed unit timelike normal, characterized by orthogonality to $T\Sigma$, $g(\nu,\nu)=-1$ and $g(\nu,N)<0$; the Cauchy data of a smooth $u$ are $u|_\Sigma$ and the normal derivative $\nu(u)|_\Sigma$. The uniqueness condition is that a smooth solution of $Pu=0$ with both data zero on $\Sigma$ is zero.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(M,g,N,P,E_+,E_-)$ be a Green-data interface. Put $\mathcal D_g(M)=C_c^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$, $V(M):=\mathcal D_g(M)/P\mathcal D_g(M)$, and, for $[f],[h]\in V(M)$, define

$$\sigma_M([f],[h]):=\int_M f(Eh)\,\mu_g,$$

with $E=E_--E_+$. Then $E\mathcal D_g(M)\subseteq\operatorname{Sol}_{\mathrm{sc}}(M)$, $\ker E=P\mathcal D_g(M)$, and $\sigma_M$ is a well-defined nondegenerate real alternating bilinear form on $V(M)$. Thus $V(M)$ is a real symplectic vector space. This statement does not assert that $E\mathcal D_g(M)=\operatorname{Sol}_{\mathrm{sc}}(M)$.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $(M,g,N)$ and $P=-\Box_g+V$ have the smooth geometric and scalar-operator hypotheses of the Green-data definition, with arbitrary real $V\in C^\infty(M)$. No Green maps are assumed. Choose a smooth Cauchy temporal splitting $M=\mathbb R\times S$, $g=-\alpha^2dt^2+h_t$, with $\alpha>0$, and write $S_a=\{t=a\}$ and $\nu=\alpha^{-1}\partial_t$. For every $a\in\mathbb R$, $u_0,u_1\in C_c^\infty(S_a;\mathbb R)$ and $f\in C_c^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ there is a unique smooth solution

$$Pu=f,\qquad u|_{S_a}=u_0,\qquad \nu(u)|_{S_a}=u_1.$$

For $t\ge a$ its support is contained in $J^+(K_+)$, where $K_+=\operatorname{supp}u_0\cup\operatorname{supp}u_1\cup(\operatorname{supp}f\cap\{t\ge a\})$; the time-reversed assertion holds for $t\le a$. These are supports in the indicated closed half-spacetimes. On every finite time slab these support sets are compact. For fixed compact input supports, each compact-output derivative seminorm of $u$ is bounded by a constant times a finite sum of input derivative seminorms. For every Cauchy set $\Sigma$ and point $q$, the set $J^-(q)\cap J^+(\Sigma)$ and its time reverse are compact. Finally, on every smooth spacelike Cauchy hypersurface $\Sigma$, a smooth homogeneous solution with $u|_\Sigma=\nu(u)|_\Sigma=0$ vanishes identically, without a support hypothesis on that solution.

derivations.claim: Every volume-time level $S_c$ of $U$ is also a Cauchy set of $M$. Let $\gamma$ be any inextendible causal curve in $M$. It meets the Cauchy hypersurface $\Sigma\subset U$ from the Cauchy-morphism hypothesis. Because $U$ is causally convex, $\gamma^{-1}(U)$ is an interval: if two parameter values lie in $U$, the causal segment between them lies in $U$. The restriction of $\gamma$ to this interval is inextendible in $U$; a limit at a boundary point of the interval in $U$ would, by openness and continuity, extend the interval, while a limit at an end of the original curve would contradict its inextendibility in $M$. Hence this restriction meets the Cauchy level $S_c$ of $U$ exactly once by [F1]. This proves the claim for every $c$.

Choose any $a<b$. The two open sets $I^+(S_a)$ and $I^-(S_b)$ cover $M$. To see this, take a maximal future timelike geodesic through any point $p\in M$ using [F6]. By step 1.1 it meets both Cauchy levels, and it meets $S_a$ before $S_b$: between the two crossings the curve lies in $U$ by causal convexity, where $t_U$ strictly increases from $a$ to $b$ [F1,F7]. If $p$ is strictly after the $S_a$ crossing then $p\in I^+(S_a)$; otherwise it is strictly before the $S_b$ crossing and $p\in I^-(S_b)$. Openness follows from [F5]. Apply [F4] to obtain smooth $\theta_+,\theta_-:M\to[0,1]$ with $\theta_++\theta_-=1$, $\operatorname{supp}\theta_+\subset I^+(S_a)$ and $\operatorname{supp}\theta_-\subset I^-(S_b)$. Set $f_\pm:=\theta_\pm f$ and $K_\pm:=\operatorname{supp}f_\pm$; these are compact, and $K_\pm$ lie in the stated open sets.

If $K_+$ is nonempty, choose $a'>a$ with $K_+\subset I^+_M(S_{a'})$, as follows. The opens $I^+_M(S_c)$ for $c>a$ cover $I^+_M(S_a)$: a timelike curve from $S_a$ to a point of this latter set has a short initial segment inside the open $U$, on which $t_U$ increases above $a$ and crosses some level $c>a$ before reaching the endpoint. For a finite subcover of the compact $K_+$ choose $a'$ between $a$ and the least selected $c$; ordering of the levels then gives the asserted containment. This never evaluates $t_U$ outside $U$. The sets $A:=J^-_M(S_a)$ and $B:=J^+_M(S_{a'})$ are closed and disjoint: any causal segment from the later level to the earlier one would stay in $U$ and contradict strict increase of $t_U$. A smooth partition for $M\setminus A$ and $M\setminus B$ gives $\rho_+:M\to[0,1]$ equal to zero near $A$ and one near $B$, with $\operatorname{supp}\rho_+\subset M\setminus A$ and $\operatorname{supp}(d\rho_+)\subset M\setminus(A\cup B)$. Every point in that transition set is causally between $S_a$ and $S_{a'}$, because both are Cauchy sets of $M$; causal convexity puts this transition set inside $U$. The larger shadow $H_+:=J^+_M(S_a)\cap J^-_M(K_+)$ is compact in $M$: cover $K_+$ by finitely many open chronological pasts $I^-_M(q_j)$, use transitivity to enclose $H_+$ in $\bigcup_j(J^-(q_j)\cap J^+(S_a))$, compact by [F9], and use closedness from [F2] and [F3]. The shadow need not lie in $U$. Put $\psi_+:=\rho_+E_-f_+$. Its closed support lies in $H_+$, so $\psi_+\in\mathcal D_g(M)$. Since $\rho_+=1$ near $K_+$, the product rule gives $g_+:=f_+-P\psi_+=-[P,\rho_+]E_-f_+$, with $[P,\rho]u:=P(\rho u)-\rho Pu$. Its support lies in the transition set inside $U$ and in the compact shadow $H_+$, so $g_+$ has compact support in $U$. By [F8], $Eg_+=Ef_+$. If $K_+=\varnothing$, set $g_+=0$.

The time-reversed construction applies to $K_-\subset I^-_M(S_b)$. In detail, the opens $I^-_M(S_c)$ for $c<b$ cover $I^-_M(S_b)$ by taking a short terminal timelike segment inside $U$; a finite subcover selects $b'<b$ with $K_-\subset I^-_M(S_{b'})$. A partition for the complements of the closed disjoint sets $A':=J^-_M(S_{b'})$ and $B':=J^+_M(S_b)$ gives $\rho_-=1$ near $A'$, $\rho_-=0$ near $B'$, and $\operatorname{supp}\rho_-\subset M\setminus B'$. Its derivative support lies causally between the two levels and hence inside $U$. The shadow $H_-:=J^+_M(K_-)\cap J^-_M(S_b)$ is compact by the reversed [F9], a finite cover of $K_-$ by chronological futures, and closedness, just as in step 3.1. Define $\psi_-:=\rho_-E_+f_-\in\mathcal D_g(M)$ and $g_-:=f_--P\psi_-=-[P,\rho_-]E_+f_-$. The support of $g_-$ is closed, contained in $H_-$ and in the transition set inside $U$, so it is compact in $U$; [F8] gives $Eg_-=Ef_-$. The zero-support case uses $g_-=0$.

Let $g_U$ be the restriction to $U$ of $g:=g_++g_-$, whose two summands have compact support in $U$ by steps 3.1 and 4.1. Then $\iota_*g_U=g$, and $Eg=Eg_++Eg_-=Ef_++Ef_-=Ef$ by those same steps and $f=f_++f_-$. By [F8], $\ker E=P\mathcal D_g(M)$, so $E(f-\iota_*g_U)=0$ implies $f-\iota_*g_U\in P\mathcal D_g(M)$. This is the asserted equality of test classes.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), with the pointwise causal
classification of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and the
equivalence of "future-directed" with "pairing negatively with $N$" supplied by
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]. All curves below
take values in $M$; the physical reading of the model is not part of this
definition.

**(a) The curve class.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a continuous map,
where $I$ has its relative topology. A **chart representative** on a parameter
neighborhood $J\subseteq I$ is $x\circ\gamma|_J$, where $(U,x)$ is a smooth
chart and $\gamma(J)\subseteq U$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]). The map $\gamma$ is
**locally absolutely continuous** when for each $t\in I$ there are
$\delta>0$ and a chart $(U,x)$ such that
$\gamma(I\cap(t-\delta,t+\delta))\subseteq U$ and every coordinate of
$x\circ\gamma$ is absolutely continuous on every compact subinterval of
$I\cap(t-\delta,t+\delta)$ in the sense of
[[def-absolutely-continuous-function]]. This includes one-sided neighborhoods
at included endpoints. Equivalently, for every compact subinterval
$[a,b]\subseteq I$ and every chart $(U,x)$ with
$\gamma([a,b])\subseteq U$, the coordinates of $x\circ\gamma$ are
absolutely continuous on $[a,b]$. The equivalence and independence of the
chart and smooth atlas are proved in [[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]]
clause (a); continuity is part of both formulations.

**(b) Velocity and causal curves.** Let $\gamma$ be locally absolutely
continuous and let $t$ be an interior point of $I$ at which some — equivalently
every — chart representative is differentiable. The **velocity**
$\gamma'(t)\in T_{\gamma(t)}M$ is the derivation whose components in a chart
$(U,x)$ around $\gamma(t)$ are
$\gamma'(t)=\sum_{a=0}^{3}\frac{d}{dt}(x^a\circ\gamma)(t)\,\partial_a|_{\gamma(t)}$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]],
[[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]); it is independent of the
chart by the chain rule, as recorded in
[[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (b). A **future causal curve** is a
locally absolutely continuous $\gamma$ such that the set of $t\in I$ for which
$\gamma'(t)$ exists, is nonzero and is future causal is of full measure in
$I$ (its complement meets every compact subinterval of $I$ in a set of
Lebesgue measure zero). A **future timelike curve** (also called future
chronological) is defined in the same way with "future causal" replaced by
"future timelike". Past-directed versions are defined with $g_p(v,N_p)>0$.
Since a future causal nonzero vector is nonzero by definition, the velocity is
required to be nonzero at almost every parameter value; in particular no
nondegenerate subinterval of $I$ can be mapped to a single point: a
constant chart representative has derivative zero everywhere in its interior,
contradicting the full-measure nonzero-velocity requirement.

**(c) Reachability.** For events $p,q\in M$ define:

- $p\le q$, read "$q$ is in the future of $p$", when $p=q$, or when there are
  $a<b$ and a future causal curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$;
- $p\ll q$, read "$p$ chronologically precedes $q$", when there are $a<b$ and
  a future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$.

The **causal future** and **chronological future** of a subset $S\subseteq M$
are
$$J^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}J^+(p),\qquad I^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}I^+(p),$$
where $J^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\le q\}$ and $I^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\ll q\}$; past
versions are $J^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ q\in J^+(p)\}$ and
$I^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ p\ll q\}$. By the displayed definition
$p\in J^+(p)$ for every $p$. Whether $p\in I^+(p)$ is a property of the
model, not a convention: $p\ll p$ holds exactly when there are $a<b$ and a
future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)=p$, that
is, exactly when a closed future timelike curve through $p$ exists. No
irreflexivity of $\ll$ is asserted, and closed timelike curves are not
excluded by the definition.

**(d) Inextendibility.** A locally absolutely continuous causal curve
$\gamma:I\to M$ is **future-inextendible** when $\gamma$ does not converge to
any point of $M$ as its parameter tends to $\sup I$, that is, there is no
$x\in M$ with $\gamma(t)\to x$ as $t\to\sup I$; in particular a curve whose
parameter range is unbounded above is future-inextendible exactly when it does
not converge as $t\to+\infty$. **Past-inextendible** is defined dually with
$\inf I$, and $\gamma$ is **inextendible** when it is both. This is the
convention of Minguzzi's Definition 2.16; for causal curves parametrized by
arclength of a complete auxiliary Riemannian metric it agrees with "the domain
cannot be extended", and a causal curve that converges at an endpoint can be
extended by a short geodesic segment, as proved in
[[lem-gr-maximal-geodesics-and-extension]] clauses (a) and (b). A causal
curve **passes through** $p$ when $p\in\gamma(I)$.

**(e) Scope.** The definitions are mathematical. They record no postulate
about nature, no measurement and no dynamical law; the physical reading of
$(M,g,N)$ and of the causal structure as the model's signalling structure is
adopted in the framework postulates and is not asserted here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in its first argument ([[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Write $\mathcal B(H)$ for the bounded linear operators on $H$ ([[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]); for $M\in\mathcal B(H)$, $M^*$ is its Hilbert adjoint, characterized by $\langle Mx,y\rangle=\langle x,M^*y\rangle$ ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]).

Under this same $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ hypothesis, [[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]] gives $M^*\in\mathcal B(H)$ and $\|M^*\|=\|M\|$.

A **finite bounded Kraus instrument datum** on $H$ consists of an integer $m\ge1$, integers $q_a\ge0$ for $a=1,\ldots,m$, and bounded operators $M_{a,r}\in\mathcal B(H)$ for $r=1,\ldots,q_a$. It is **normalized** when

$$\sum_{a=1}^{m}\sum_{r=1}^{q_a}M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}=I_H.$$

Empty inner sums are zero. For each outcome $a$, define its outcome operator and operation by

$$E_a:=\sum_{r=1}^{q_a}M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r},\qquad \mathcal J_a(X):=\sum_{r=1}^{q_a}M_{a,r}XM_{a,r}^*\quad(X\in\mathcal B(H)).$$

These formulas take values in $\mathcal B(H)$: the adjoint theorem above makes each $M_{a,r}^*$ bounded, and $\|M_{a,r}XM_{a,r}^*x\|\le\|M_{a,r}\|\,\|X\|\,\|M_{a,r}^*\|\,\|x\|=\|M_{a,r}\|^2\,\|X\|\,\|x\|$; the sums are finite. This definition specifies only the displayed finite Kraus form; it is not a representation theorem for arbitrary instruments and does not assert that an apparatus realizes these data.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ carry a normalized finite bounded Kraus instrument datum as defined in [[def-qft-finite-bounded-kraus-instrument]], and let $\rho$ be a density operator on $H$: a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]], [[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). For each outcome $a$, put $p_a:=\operatorname{tr}(\mathcal J_a(\rho))$. Then each $E_a$ is an effect ($E_a\ge0$ and $I_H-E_a\ge0$), each $\mathcal J_a(\rho)$ is positive trace class, and

$$p_a=\operatorname{tr}(\mathcal J_a(\rho))=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_a)\in[0,1],\qquad \sum_{a=1}^{m}p_a=1.$$

The nonselective output $\sum_a\mathcal J_a(\rho)$ is a density operator. If $p_a>0$, the normalized conditional state $\rho_a:=\mathcal J_a(\rho)/p_a$ is a density operator; when $p_a=0$, this normalized update is undefined. For a unit vector $\psi\in H$, the rank-one density operator $\rho=T_{\psi,\psi}$ has outcome probability $p_a=\sum_{r=1}^{q_a}\|M_{a,r}\psi\|^2$. These are conditional mathematical identities; they do not assert that an apparatus realizes the instrument or supply a physical measurement postulate.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and for $u,v\in H$ let $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]).

(a) For every bounded $B\in\mathcal B(H)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]),

$$BT_{u,v}=T_{Bu,v},\qquad T_{u,v}B=T_{u,B^*v},$$

with the Hilbert adjoint $B^*$ ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]).

(b) Let $T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class and let $T=\sum_jT_{u_j,v_j}$ be a nuclear representation, i.e. the partial sums converge to $T$ in operator norm and $\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|<\infty$ ([[lem-nuclear-series-characterizes-trace-norm]], [[def-trace-class-operator]]). Then for every bounded $B$

$$\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\sum_j\langle Bu_j,v_j\rangle,\qquad \operatorname{tr}(TB)=\sum_j\langle u_j,B^*v_j\rangle,$$

both series converging absolutely with $\bigl|\operatorname{tr}(BT)\bigr|\le\|B\|\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|$, and $\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\operatorname{tr}(TB)$ ([[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]). In particular $\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\operatorname{tr}(TB)$ for every trace-class $T$ and bounded $B$, and $\operatorname{tr}(T_{u,v})=\langle u,v\rangle$. No cyclic permutation of unbounded operators is asserted.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]].
Let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ be open. For real
$f\in C_c^\infty(O)$ define
$$W_\mu(f):=W_{\rm Segal}(\sqrt2K_\mu f),$$
where the Segal normalization is exactly
$\Phi_{\rm Segal}(h)=(a^\dagger(h)+a(h))/\sqrt2$ on the finite-particle
domain, as in [[lem-qft-segal-weyl-domain]]. This scale makes the self-adjoint generator
of $t\mapsto W_\mu(tf)$ equal to the closure $\overline{\Phi_\mu(f)}$,
whose restriction to $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is the real scalar field
$\Phi_\mu(f)=a(K_\mu f)+a^\dagger(K_\mu f)$ of
[[lem-qft-smeared-free-scalar]]. Define the unital norm-closed operator
algebra
$$\mathfrak A_\mu(O)= \overline{\operatorname{alg}}^{\|\cdot\|} \{I,W_\mu(f),W_\mu(f)^*:f\in C_c^\infty(O;\mathbb R)\}.$$
Then $O_1\subseteq O_2$ implies
$\mathfrak A_\mu(O_1)\subseteq\mathfrak A_\mu(O_2)$. If every difference
$x-y$, with $x\in O_1$ and $y\in O_2$, is spacelike, then every element of
$\mathfrak A_\mu(O_1)$ commutes with every element of
$\mathfrak A_\mu(O_2)$. These are algebraic properties of the constructed
representation; they are not empirical signaling or measurement claims.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $(M,g,N,P,E_+,E_-)$ be a Green-data background of [[def-qftx-green-hyperbolic-interface]], and let $\mathfrak W_M(O)$ be the algebraic local Weyl subalgebra assigned to an open set $O\subseteq M$ by [[def-qftx-free-weyl-net]]. If $O_1\subseteq O_2$, then $\mathfrak W_M(O_1)\subseteq\mathfrak W_M(O_2)$. If $O_1$ and $O_2$ are causally disjoint, meaning that no point of either set is causally related in either direction to a point of the other, then every element of $\mathfrak W_M(O_1)$ commutes with every element of $\mathfrak W_M(O_2)$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
(Real and imaginary parts, complex conjugation, and modulus). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of Real and complex inner product spaces, with the inner product linear in the first argument: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published The norm $\lVert v\rVert=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ induced by a real or complex inner product: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space and let $\mathcal A,\mathcal B\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be unital $*$-subalgebras (each contains $I_H$ and is closed under adjoints and linear combinations) such that $AC=CA$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$ and $C\in\mathcal B$. Let $M_1,\ldots,M_n\in\mathcal A$ be a finite family, $n\ge1$, satisfying
$$\sum_{r=1}^n M_r^*M_r=I_H.$$
For any state $\omega$ on $\mathcal B(H)$, meaning a complex-linear functional with $\omega(I_H)=1$ and $\omega(X^*X)\in[0,\infty)$ for every $X\in\mathcal B(H)$, define the nonselective expectation on $C\in\mathcal B$ by
$$\omega'(C):=\sum_{r=1}^n\omega(M_r^*CM_r).$$
Then $\omega'(C)=\omega(C)$ for every $C\in\mathcal B$. This is an algebraic conditional deduction; it does not assert that a physical apparatus realizes these operators.

For the finite flat scalar mass-shell representation of [[lem-qft-scalar-local-weyl-algebra]], open regions whose point differences are all spacelike have commuting local Weyl algebras, so the proposition applies to those two algebras. The proposition itself only assumes the stated commutation relation and does not require a tensor-product factorization of $H$.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ whose induced-length metric is complete: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm (Banach space).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
Banach space defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Let $X$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and assume
$X$ admits an ordered basis of finite length. Then $X$ is a Banach space in the
sense of [[def-banach-space]].

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field. Write

$$\mathcal B(X,Y) := \{T:X\to Y : T \text{ is a bounded linear operator}\}.$$

This is a subspace of the vector space $\mathcal L(X,Y)$ of
[[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]], with the same pointwise operations:

$$(S+T)(x) := Sx+Tx,\qquad (\lambda T)(x) := \lambda\,Tx.$$

If $X=Y$, write

$$\mathcal B(X) := \mathcal B(X,X).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ and $K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a bounded linear operator ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For fixed $y\in K$ the map

$$x\longmapsto\langle Tx,y\rangle_K$$

is a bounded linear functional on $H$: it is linear in $x$ because $T$ is linear and the pairing is linear in its first argument, and $|\langle Tx,y\rangle_K|\le\|Tx\|\,\|y\|\le\|T\|\,\|x\|\,\|y\|$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and the operator-norm inequality ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]], [[def-operator-norm]]). By Riesz representation ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) there is therefore a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with

$$\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H\qquad\text{for every }x\in H .$$

The **Hilbert adjoint** of $T$ is the map

$$T^*:K\longrightarrow H,\qquad y\longmapsto T^*y .$$

It is the unique map $K\to H$ satisfying the displayed identity, since two such maps have $\langle x,(T^*_1-T^*_2)y\rangle=0$ for all $x$ and hence $(T^*_1-T^*_2)y=0$ by positive definiteness.

**The dictionary with the Banach transpose.** Write $R_H:H\to H^*$ and $R_K:K\to K^*$ for the Riesz maps $R_H(x)=\langle\,\cdot\,,x\rangle_H$ and $R_K(y)=\langle\,\cdot\,,y\rangle_K$, and let $T'\in\mathcal B(K^*,H^*)$ be the transpose of $T$, $(T'g)(x)=g(Tx)$ ([[def-transpose-of-a-bounded-operator]]). Then for all $y\in K$ and $x\in H$,

$$\bigl(R_H(T^*y)\bigr)(x)=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H=\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=(R_Ky)(Tx)=\bigl(T'(R_Ky)\bigr)(x),$$

so $R_H\,T^*=T'\,R_K$. The Hilbert adjoint is thus the Banach transpose conjugated by the Riesz identifications of $H$ and $K$ with their duals; it is a different operator from $T'$ whenever the Riesz maps are conjugate-linear.

The four vectors $|ab\rangle$ are orthonormal, so $\|\psi\|^2=(1+1)/2=1$. By [F1], $\omega$ is complex-linear and $\omega(I_H)=1$. For every $X\in\mathcal B(H)$, adjointness [F5] and conjugate symmetry give $\omega(X^*X)=\langle X^*X\psi,\psi\rangle=\overline{\langle\psi,X^*X\psi\rangle}=\overline{\langle X\psi,X\psi\rangle}=\|X\psi\|^2\ge0$, so $\omega$ is a state in the sense of [F2]. The projections satisfy $M_0^*=M_0$, $M_1^*=M_1$, $M_0M_1=0$, and $M_0+M_1=I_H$. Hence $\sum_{j=0}^1M_j^*M_j=I_H$, and
$$M_0\psi=\frac{|00\rangle}{\sqrt2},\qquad M_1\psi=\frac{|11\rangle}{\sqrt2}.$$
The outcome probabilities are $p_j=\|M_j\psi\|^2=1/2$, so both normalized conditional vectors are defined.

Dividing the branch vectors in step 1.1 by $\sqrt{p_j}=1/\sqrt2$ gives $\psi_0=|00\rangle$ and $\psi_1=|11\rangle$. Since $Z_B|00\rangle=|00\rangle$ and $Z_B|11\rangle=-|11\rangle$, their conditional expectations are respectively $\omega_0(Z_B)=\langle Z_B\psi_0,\psi_0\rangle=+1$ and $\omega_1(Z_B)=\langle Z_B\psi_1,\psi_1\rangle=-1$. Also
$$Z_B\psi=\frac{|00\rangle-|11\rangle}{\sqrt2},\qquad \omega(Z_B)=\langle Z_B\psi,\psi\rangle=\left\langle\frac{|00\rangle-|11\rangle}{\sqrt2},\frac{|00\rangle+|11\rangle}{\sqrt2}\right\rangle=0,$$
because the cross terms vanish by orthogonality.

Let $\mathcal A:=\{A\otimes I_2:A\in\mathcal B(\mathbb C^2)\}$ and $\mathcal B:=\{I_2\otimes B:B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb C^2)\}$. For every elementary tensor $u\otimes v$, $(A\otimes I_2)(I_2\otimes B)(u\otimes v)=Au\otimes Bv=(I_2\otimes B)(A\otimes I_2)(u\otimes v)$; elementary tensors span $H$, so these unital $*$-algebras commute. The two projections lie in $\mathcal A$ and the normalization was checked in step 1.1. Applying [F2] to the state proved in step 1.1 and $C=Z_B$ gives the nonselective expectation $\sum_j\omega(M_j^*Z_BM_j)=\sum_j\langle M_j^*Z_BM_j\psi,\psi\rangle=\omega(Z_B)=\langle Z_B\psi,\psi\rangle=0$. Equivalently, the probability-weighted conditional values from step 2.1 average to $(1/2)(+1)+(1/2)(-1)=0$. Thus post-selection changes the conditional remote expectation in either branch, while retaining and averaging the outcomes leaves the original remote marginal unchanged.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with the
causal curves and the relations $\le$, $\ll$, $I^{\pm}$, $J^{\pm}$ of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]]. All curves below are curves in
that sense.

**(a) Chronology and causality.** $(M,g,N)$ is **chronological** when there is
no $p\in M$ with $p\ll p$, equivalently when there is no nonconstant future
timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)$. It is **causal**
when there is no nonconstant future causal curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with
$\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)$; a nonconstant future causal curve with equal endpoints
is called a **closed causal curve**, and a closed future timelike curve is
called a **closed timelike curve**.

**(b) Strong causality.** $(M,g,N)$ is **strongly causal** when for every
$p\in M$ and every open set $U\subseteq M$ with $p\in U$ there is an open set
$V$ with $p\in V\subseteq U$ such that for every future causal curve
$\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ and all $a\le s<t\le b$ with $\gamma(s)\in V$ and
$\gamma(t)\in V$ one has $\gamma([s,t])\subseteq V$. Thus no causal curve can
leave $V$ and later re-enter it; a set $V$ with this property for all causal
curves is called **causally convex for causal curves that meet it twice**.

**(c) Global hyperbolicity.** $(M,g,N)$ is **globally hyperbolic** when it is
strongly causal and for all $p,q\in M$ the **causal diamond**
$J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)$ is compact in the subspace topology
([[def-compact-space]]).

**(d) Time functions.** A **time function** on $(M,g,N)$ is a function
$u:M\to\mathbb R$ which is continuous from the manifold topology to the usual topology of
$\mathbb R$: for every $p\in M$ and every open neighborhood $W$ of $u(p)$
there is an open neighborhood $V$ of $p$ with $u(V)\subseteq W$
([[def-continuous-map-top]]). It also satisfies
$u(\gamma(a))<u(\gamma(b))$ for every future causal curve
$\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $a<b$ that is not constant on $[a,b]$.

**(e) Temporal functions.** A **temporal function** on $(M,g,N)$ is a smooth
function $u:M\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]])
whose gradient is past-directed timelike: writing $du$ for its differential
([[def-differential-of-a-smooth-map]]) and $\nabla u$ for the vector field
with $g(\nabla u,X)=du(X)$ for every smooth vector field $X$, constructed from
the inverse metric of [[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]], one
has
$$g(\nabla u,\nabla u)<0\qquad\text{and}\qquad du(N)=g(\nabla u,N)>0 .$$
The first inequality says that the gradient is nowhere zero and timelike; the
second fixes it as past-directed for the chosen time orientation. No level set
of a temporal function is asserted here to be a hypersurface or to be
spacelike, and no relation between temporal functions and compactness is
asserted; those claims are proved separately where they are used.

**(f) Scope and conventions.** These are mathematical conditions on the
Lorentzian model. Different sources define global hyperbolicity by equivalent
but differently phrased conditions; this page fixes the formulation of (c)
and proves the implications it uses. In particular no equivalence between
global hyperbolicity and the existence of a Cauchy hypersurface is asserted
by this definition, and the physical reading of strong causality or global
hyperbolicity as predictability of a classical model is adopted only in the
framework postulates.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), with the pointwise causal
classification of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and the
equivalence of "future-directed" with "pairing negatively with $N$" supplied by
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]. All curves below
take values in $M$; the physical reading of the model is not part of this
definition.

**(a) The curve class.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a continuous map,
where $I$ has its relative topology. A **chart representative** on a parameter
neighborhood $J\subseteq I$ is $x\circ\gamma|_J$, where $(U,x)$ is a smooth
chart and $\gamma(J)\subseteq U$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]). The map $\gamma$ is
**locally absolutely continuous** when for each $t\in I$ there are
$\delta>0$ and a chart $(U,x)$ such that
$\gamma(I\cap(t-\delta,t+\delta))\subseteq U$ and every coordinate of
$x\circ\gamma$ is absolutely continuous on every compact subinterval of
$I\cap(t-\delta,t+\delta)$ in the sense of
[[def-absolutely-continuous-function]]. This includes one-sided neighborhoods
at included endpoints. Equivalently, for every compact subinterval
$[a,b]\subseteq I$ and every chart $(U,x)$ with
$\gamma([a,b])\subseteq U$, the coordinates of $x\circ\gamma$ are
absolutely continuous on $[a,b]$. The equivalence and independence of the
chart and smooth atlas are proved in [[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]]
clause (a); continuity is part of both formulations.

**(b) Velocity and causal curves.** Let $\gamma$ be locally absolutely
continuous and let $t$ be an interior point of $I$ at which some — equivalently
every — chart representative is differentiable. The **velocity**
$\gamma'(t)\in T_{\gamma(t)}M$ is the derivation whose components in a chart
$(U,x)$ around $\gamma(t)$ are
$\gamma'(t)=\sum_{a=0}^{3}\frac{d}{dt}(x^a\circ\gamma)(t)\,\partial_a|_{\gamma(t)}$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]],
[[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]); it is independent of the
chart by the chain rule, as recorded in
[[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (b). A **future causal curve** is a
locally absolutely continuous $\gamma$ such that the set of $t\in I$ for which
$\gamma'(t)$ exists, is nonzero and is future causal is of full measure in
$I$ (its complement meets every compact subinterval of $I$ in a set of
Lebesgue measure zero). A **future timelike curve** (also called future
chronological) is defined in the same way with "future causal" replaced by
"future timelike". Past-directed versions are defined with $g_p(v,N_p)>0$.
Since a future causal nonzero vector is nonzero by definition, the velocity is
required to be nonzero at almost every parameter value; in particular no
nondegenerate subinterval of $I$ can be mapped to a single point: a
constant chart representative has derivative zero everywhere in its interior,
contradicting the full-measure nonzero-velocity requirement.

**(c) Reachability.** For events $p,q\in M$ define:

- $p\le q$, read "$q$ is in the future of $p$", when $p=q$, or when there are
  $a<b$ and a future causal curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$;
- $p\ll q$, read "$p$ chronologically precedes $q$", when there are $a<b$ and
  a future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$.

The **causal future** and **chronological future** of a subset $S\subseteq M$
are
$$J^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}J^+(p),\qquad I^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}I^+(p),$$
where $J^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\le q\}$ and $I^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\ll q\}$; past
versions are $J^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ q\in J^+(p)\}$ and
$I^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ p\ll q\}$. By the displayed definition
$p\in J^+(p)$ for every $p$. Whether $p\in I^+(p)$ is a property of the
model, not a convention: $p\ll p$ holds exactly when there are $a<b$ and a
future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)=p$, that
is, exactly when a closed future timelike curve through $p$ exists. No
irreflexivity of $\ll$ is asserted, and closed timelike curves are not
excluded by the definition.

**(d) Inextendibility.** A locally absolutely continuous causal curve
$\gamma:I\to M$ is **future-inextendible** when $\gamma$ does not converge to
any point of $M$ as its parameter tends to $\sup I$, that is, there is no
$x\in M$ with $\gamma(t)\to x$ as $t\to\sup I$; in particular a curve whose
parameter range is unbounded above is future-inextendible exactly when it does
not converge as $t\to+\infty$. **Past-inextendible** is defined dually with
$\inf I$, and $\gamma$ is **inextendible** when it is both. This is the
convention of Minguzzi's Definition 2.16; for causal curves parametrized by
arclength of a complete auxiliary Riemannian metric it agrees with "the domain
cannot be extended", and a causal curve that converges at an endpoint can be
extended by a short geodesic segment, as proved in
[[lem-gr-maximal-geodesics-and-extension]] clauses (a) and (b). A causal
curve **passes through** $p$ when $p\in\gamma(I)$.

**(e) Scope.** The definitions are mathematical. They record no postulate
about nature, no measurement and no dynamical law; the physical reading of
$(M,g,N)$ and of the causal structure as the model's signalling structure is
adopted in the framework postulates and is not asserted here.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]).

- An **open cover** of $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is a family
  $\mathcal{U} \subseteq \mathcal{T}$ of open sets with $X = \bigcup \mathcal{U}$,
  where $\bigcup \mathcal{U} = \{\, x \in X : x \in U \text{ for some } U \in \mathcal{U} \,\}$.
- A **subcover** of $\mathcal{U}$ is a subfamily $\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{U}$
  that is itself an open cover.
- A family $\mathcal{V}$ of sets is **finite** when $\mathcal{V} = \varnothing$ or
  there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sets $V_0, \dots, V_n$ with
  $\mathcal{V} = \{V_0, \dots, V_n\}$; repetitions in the list are allowed and
  harmless.
- $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is **compact** when every open cover of it has a finite
  subcover: for every open cover $\mathcal{U}$, either $X = \varnothing$ and the
  empty subfamily covers it, or there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
  $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with
  $$X = U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n .$$
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **compact subset** of $X$ when the subspace
  $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ is a compact topological space, $\mathcal{T}_A$ being the
  subspace topology ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

**Compactness of a subset is defined intrinsically, and only intrinsically.**
The last clause speaks about the subspace $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ and its own open
sets, not about families of open subsets of the ambient $X$. The two readings do
agree, but that is a theorem and not a convention: it is
[[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]], and no item of this library may use
the ambient reading without citing it. Taking the intrinsic reading makes
compactness a property of the topological space $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ alone.
Hence it is preserved when $A$ is embedded homeomorphically as a subspace, or
when another ambient space induces the same topology on $A$; it need not be
preserved if the induced topology changes. This is exactly the convention already fixed for
metric spaces by [[def-metric-compactness]], and the agreement of that
definition with this one is [[thm-compactness-agrees-with-metric-compactness]].

**The empty space is compact**, since the empty subfamily of any family covers
it; this is the reason the clause above is written with the two cases. Every
space listed as $\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$ is compact too: given a cover, each $x_i$
lies in some member, and finitely many members named in this way already cover.
So every finite space is compact, whatever its topology, and in particular the
discrete topology on a finite set is compact while the discrete topology on an
infinite set is not ([[def-standard-topologies]]).

**The finiteness convention.** "Finite" above is the listing form. It agrees with
the definition of finiteness by equinumerosity with a natural number
([[def-countable]]), in both directions, and the agreement is the one already
discharged in [[def-metric-compactness]]: a nonempty set equinumerous with
$m \ge 1$ is listable, and a set listed as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$ injects into
$\sigma(n)$ by sending $x$ to the least $i \le n$ with $a_i = x$. Neither
direction uses a choice principle; the second selects nothing, taking a least
index instead.

**Quasicompact is not used here.** Some authors, following Bourbaki, reserve
*compact* for a space that is both compact in the above sense and Hausdorff, and
call the open-cover condition alone *quasicompact*. This library follows the more
widely adopted convention: **compact** means the open-cover condition and nothing
more, and a Hausdorff hypothesis is always written out. The fork is recorded in
[[rem-compactness-conventions-and-choice-ledger]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), as used to form the time-oriented Lorentzian geometric data below. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a Hausdorff, second-countable, oriented and time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold without boundary, with signature $(-,+,+,+)$, and assume it is globally hyperbolic in the convention of [[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]]: strongly causal and with compact causal diamonds. Curves and the causal sets $J^\pm(K)$ use the locally absolutely continuous causal-curve convention of [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]].

Write the positive metric density in a chart as $\mu_g=|\det(g_{ab})|^{1/2}|dx^0dx^1dx^2dx^3|$. This is a coordinate-independent smooth density: if $y=\psi(x)$, then $g_y=(D\psi^{-1})^Tg_xD\psi^{-1}$, so $|\det(g_y)|^{1/2}=|\det D\psi^{-1}|\,|\det(g_x)|^{1/2}$, the test-density transformation rule of [[def-qftx-distributions-on-smooth-manifolds]]. Let $\mathcal D_g(M):=C_c^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ have the real test-function topology transported by $f\mapsto f\mu_g$ from that supplier's compactly supported smooth test densities. Give $C^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ its usual topology of uniform convergence of every coordinate derivative on each compact subset.

For a real $V\in C^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ define the scalar Klein–Gordon-type operator $P=-\Box_g+V$, where $\Box_g f:=\mu_g^{-1}\partial_a(\mu_g g^{ab}\partial_b f)$ in a chart. Its principal symbol is $-g^{ab}\xi_a\xi_b$. No physical units are assigned; this is a mathematical differential operator. The Green-data interface below requires formal self-adjointness with respect to $\mu_g$, meaning $\int_M f(Pu)\,\mu_g=\int_M (Pf)u\,\mu_g$ for every $f\in\mathcal D_g(M)$ and $u\in C^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$; these integrals are finite because $P$ is local. The real solution space with spacelike-compact support is

$$\operatorname{Sol}_{\mathrm{sc}}(M):=\{u\in C^\infty(M;\mathbb R): Pu=0\text{ and }\operatorname{supp}u\subseteq J^+(K)\cup J^-(K)\text{ for some compact }K\subset M\}.$$

A **Green-data interface** for $(M,g,N,P)$ consists of continuous real-linear maps $E_+,E_-:\mathcal D_g(M)\to C^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$, called respectively retarded and advanced Green maps, such that for each $f\in\mathcal D_g(M)$,

$$PE_+f=E_+Pf=f,\qquad PE_-f=E_-Pf=f,$$

$$\operatorname{supp}(E_+f)\subseteq J^+(\operatorname{supp}f),\qquad \operatorname{supp}(E_-f)\subseteq J^-(\operatorname{supp}f).$$

The interface also includes uniqueness of the smooth Cauchy problem for $P$. For a smooth spacelike Cauchy hypersurface $\Sigma$ as defined in [[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]], let $\nu$ denote its unique future-directed unit timelike normal, characterized by orthogonality to $T\Sigma$, $g(\nu,\nu)=-1$ and $g(\nu,N)<0$; the Cauchy data of a smooth $u$ are $u|_\Sigma$ and the normal derivative $\nu(u)|_\Sigma$. The uniqueness condition is that a smooth solution of $Pu=0$ with both data zero on $\Sigma$ is zero.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: (Elementary timelike coordinate neighborhoods.) At $x$ choose linear coordinates about $x$ in which $\partial_0$ is future timelike at $x$. Shrinking the coordinate box, continuity of $g$ and $N$ gives $\epsilon>0$ such that every vector with positive zeroth component and spatial-to-time coordinate ratio below $\epsilon$ is future timelike throughout that box. Choose a point $p$ on the negative time axis and a smaller open box $O_x$ about $x$, with closures inside the first box, so that every straight coordinate segment from $p$ to any point of $O_x$ has such a tangent. Then $O_x\subseteq J^+(p)$ by the definition in [F1]. The reversed construction gives an open box about $x$ contained in $J^-(q)$ for a point $q$ on its positive time axis. This uses local smooth metric continuity and straight smooth segments, without a limit-curve, global chronology-openness or dependent-choice theorem.

(Finite compact enclosure.) Take the family of all pairs of boxes and past points furnished by step 1.1 over $K$. These boxes form an open cover of $K$; taking a finite subcover names finitely many $p_i$ with $K\subseteq\bigcup_iJ^+(p_i)$. No past-point choice for an infinite family is made. Similarly take finitely many $q_j$ with $L\subseteq\bigcup_jJ^-(q_j)$. Concatenating the finite causal segments as in [F1] proves transitivity directly, so
$$J^+(K)\cap J^-(L)\subseteq\bigcup_{i,j}\bigl(J^+(p_i)\cap J^-(q_j)\bigr).$$
The right side is a finite union of compact diamonds by [F1]. Every closed subset of the left side is a closed subset of this compact union and therefore compact by [F2]. In particular $A\cap B$ is closed and has the required containment. If either input compact is empty the conclusion is immediate from the empty cover.
