Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $(M,g,N)$ be a
globally hyperbolic time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]] clause (c)), and let
$t$ be the volume time function of [[thm-gr-volume-time-function]]. Then
there exist a smooth function $T:M\to\mathbb R$ and, with $\nabla T$ the
gradient of [[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]], the
following hold.

**(a)** $T$ is a temporal function in the sense of
[[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]] clause (e): smooth,
$g(\nabla T,\nabla T)<0$ and $g(\nabla T,N)>0$ everywhere.

**(b)** Every level set $S_c:=T^{-1}(c)$, $c\in\mathbb R$, is a Cauchy
hypersurface ([[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]] clauses (a)
and (c)): it is a spacelike embedded hypersurface and every inextendible
causal curve meets it in exactly one parameter value. In particular $T$ is
surjective.

**(c)** Along every inextendible future-directed causal curve
$T\to+\infty$, and along every inextendible past-directed causal curve
$T\to-\infty$.

**(d)** The vector field $X:=\nabla T/g(\nabla T,\nabla T)$ is smooth,
future-directed timelike, satisfies $X(T)=1$, and is complete
([[def-complete-vector-field]]): every maximal integral curve of $X$ is
defined on all of $\mathbb R$, so by
[[prop-a-vector-field-is-complete-if-and-only-if-its-flow-is-global]] its
flow $\Phi:\mathbb R\times M\to M$ is a global smooth flow
([[def-local-and-global-flow]]).

**(e)** The map $\Psi:\mathbb R\times S_0\to M$, $\Psi(s,z):=\Phi(s,z)$, is
a diffeomorphism and $T(\Psi(s,z))=s$ for all $(s,z)$; equivalently $M$ is
foliated by the Cauchy hypersurfaces $S_c$, each flow line meeting each level
exactly once.

**(f)** Put $\beta:=-1/g(\nabla T,\nabla T)$, a smooth positive function, and
$h_T:=g+\beta\,dT\otimes dT$. Then $g=-\beta\,dT\otimes dT+h_T$;
$h_T(X,\cdot)=0$; and $h_T$ restricted to $\ker dT$ is a smooth Riemannian
metric, so the decomposition $T_pM=\mathbb RX_p\oplus\ker dT_p$ is
$g$-orthogonal with $g(X,X)=-\beta$. Consequently the pullback of $g$ by the
diffeomorphism $\Psi$ has no mixed terms,
$$\Psi^*g=-(\beta\circ\Psi)\,ds^2+h,\qquad h_{(s,z)}(v,w):=g_{\Phi(s,z)}\bigl((d\Phi_s)_zv,(d\Phi_s)_zw\bigr),$$
a sum of a negative definite one-dimensional form and the smooth family of
Riemannian metrics induced on the levels.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $s\ge5$ be an integer, let $A^\mu,B$ be a periodic symmetric
hyperbolic coefficient family on the open set $O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, let
$K\subseteq\operatorname{int}K'\subseteq O$ be compact, let $R\ge0$, and let
$T>0$ and $C$ be as in [[thm-gr-periodic-symmetric-hyperbolic-existence]] for
the class $\mathcal S(K,R)$; for every datum $u_0\in\mathcal S(K,R)$ let $u$ be
the solution produced there on $(-T,T)$ with values in $K'$. Then:

**(a) [local existence]** For every $u_0\in\mathcal S(K,R)$ and every
$x_0\in\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ the solution $u$ is $C^1$ on a neighborhood of
$(0,x_0)$ in $(-T,T)\times\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ and solves $(\star)$ pointwise
there.

**(b) [finite speed / independence of the extension]** Use the flat torus distance
$$d(q(x),q(y)):=\min_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}|x-y+2\pi k|.$$
In any time-independent spatial chart $y$ with a local Euclidean lift $x(y)$ of $q$, put $h_{ij}(y)=\sum_a(\partial_i x^a)(\partial_j x^a)$; this is independent of the lift, since lifts differ by constant lattice translations, and write $h^{ij}$ for its inverse. A unit spatial covector in this clause means $\xi_i\,dy^i$ with $h^{ij}\xi_i\xi_j=1$. Let $\lambda_0>0$ be
determined by the coefficient bounds on a compact set containing the values of
the solutions in the following sense: for a truncated cone
$$D:=\{(t,x):0\le t\le t_0,\ d(x,x_0)\le\lambda(t_0-t)\}$$
with $0<t_0<T$, $\lambda\ge\lambda_0$, lying in a single such spatial chart of $\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$
in which the coordinate representation of $A^\mu$ satisfies
$\lambda\,A^0+\xi_iA^i\ge0$ for every flat-metric unit covector $\xi$ at that point (such a $\lambda_0$ exists on compact coefficient sets by the norm-domination argument of clause (a) of [[lem-gr-finite-speed-independence-of-extension]], using the flat dual norm),
let $u,v$ be solutions of two periodic symmetric hyperbolic systems whose
coefficient functions agree on a neighborhood of $D$ in the independent variables and on one common open state set containing both solution ranges, with
$u(0,\cdot)=v(0,\cdot)$ on the ball $\{d(x,x_0)\le\lambda t_0\}$. Then
$u=v$ on $D$.

**(c) [local uniqueness and stability]** If two classical solutions of the same
system on a common interval have values in $K$, $H^s$ norms at most $R$ and the
same initial value, they coincide; and the continuous-dependence estimate of
[[thm-gr-periodic-symmetric-hyperbolic-uniqueness-stability]] clause (b) holds
for the solutions of clause (a).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $s\ge5$ be an integer, let $A^\mu,B$ be a periodic symmetric
hyperbolic coefficient family on the open set $O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$
([[def-gr-periodic-symmetric-hyperbolic-system]]) and let $K\subseteq O$ be
compact, and let $K'\subseteq O$ be compact with $K$ contained in the
interior of $K'$. Then for every $R\ge0$ there are a time $T>0$ and a constant
$C$ (depending on $A^\mu,B,K,K',s$ and on $R$) such that:

for every $u_0\in H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^m)$ taking values in $K$ with
$\|u_0\|_{H^s}\le R$ there is a Sobolev solution
$u:(-T,T)\to H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^m)$ of $(\star)$ with
$u(0)=u_0$ which is classical and satisfies
$$u\in L^\infty((-T,T);H^s)\cap C^0((-T,T);H^{s-1}),\quad \partial_tu\in L^\infty((-T,T);H^{s-1}),$$
$$\sup_{|t|<T}\|u(t)\|_{H^s}\le C(1+R),\qquad \sup_{|t|<T}\|\partial_tu(t)\|_{H^{s-1}}\le C(1+R),$$
and whose values lie in $K'$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $s\ge5$ be an integer, let $A^\mu,B$ be a periodic symmetric
hyperbolic coefficient family on the open set $O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, let
$K\subseteq\operatorname{int}K'\subseteq O$ be compact, let $R\ge0$, and let
$T>0$ and $C$ be as in [[thm-gr-periodic-symmetric-hyperbolic-existence]] for

of that theorem with $u(0)=u_0$ satisfies $u\in L^\infty((-T,T);H^q)$ and
$\partial_tu\in L^\infty((-T,T);H^{q-1})$ for every integer $q\ge s$, with bounds
depending only on $q$, $T$, $R$, the coefficient family, $K'$ and the $H^j$ bounds
of $u_0$ for $j\le q$; consequently $u\in C^\infty((-T,T)\times\mathbb T^3_{2\pi})$
and solves $(\star)$ classically.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let integers $s\ge m\ge0$ satisfy $s-m>3/2$, and
let $u\in H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ with the objects and notation of
[[def-gr-periodic-torus-and-sobolev-spaces]]. Then:

**(a)** There is a unique representative $u^*\in C^m(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$
of the class $u$, and for every $|\alpha|\le m$ the series
$\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(ik)^\alpha\widehat u(k)\chi_k$ converges absolutely and
uniformly on $\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ to $D^\alpha u^*$; moreover there is
$C=C(s,m,N)$ with
$$\|u^*\|_{C^m}\le C\,\|u\|_{H^s}.$$

**(b)** Writing $d(x,y):=\min\{\,|x-y+2\pi l|:l\in\mathbb Z^3\,\}$ for the
induced metric on $\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ and fixing
$0<\theta\le\min\{1,s-m-\tfrac32\}$, there is $C'=C'(s,m,N,\theta)$ with
$$\bigl|D^\alpha u^*(x)-D^\alpha u^*(y)\bigr|\le C'\,\|u\|_{H^s}\,d(x,y)^\theta\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb T^3_{2\pi},\ |\alpha|\le m).$$

**(c)** The assignment $u\mapsto u^*$ is linear; and if $(u_j)$ is a sequence in
$H^s$ with $u_j\to u$ in $H^s$, then $u_j^*\to u^*$ uniformly together with all
derivatives of order at most $m$.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]],
[[def-dependent-choice]]) for the absolutely continuous causal-curve
calculus and the supplied causal results used below.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]). Let $C\subseteq M$ be a strictly
convex normal set ([[def-gr-normal-neighborhoods-and-position-vectors]]
clause (b)), let $p\in C$, and write
$$W_p:=\exp_p^{-1}(C)\subseteq T_pM,\qquad v(q):=\exp_p^{-1}(q),\qquad P(p,q):=d(\exp_p)_{v(q)}(v(q)),\qquad D_p^2(q):=g_p(v(q),v(q)).$$
Define
$$J_C^+(p):=\{p\}\cup\{q\in C:\text{there is a future causal curve } \sigma:[0,1]\to C\text{ with }\sigma(0)=p,\ \sigma(1)=q\},$$
so the reflexive endpoint $p$ is included even though a constant curve is
not in the curve class. Define
$$I_C^+(p):=\{q\in C:\text{there is a future timelike curve } \sigma:[0,1]\to C\text{ with }\sigma(0)=p,\ \sigma(1)=q\}$$
([[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]]). Put
$$\mathcal C^+:=\{v\in W_p:v\text{ is future causal or }v=0\},\quad \mathcal T^+:=\{v\in W_p:v\text{ is future timelike}\},\quad \mathcal N^+:=\{v\in W_p:v\text{ is future null and }v\ne0\}.$$
Then:

**(a) Causal containment.** For every future causal curve
$\sigma:[0,1]\to C$ with $\sigma(0)=p$, the position vector
$v(\sigma(t))$ is future causal or zero for every $t\in[0,1]$.

**(b) Cone characterizations.**
$$J^+_C(p)=\exp_p(\mathcal C^+),\qquad I^+_C(p)=\exp_p(\mathcal T^+),\qquad J^+_C(p)\setminus\bigl(I^+_C(p)\cup\{p\}\bigr)=\exp_p(\mathcal N^+).$$

**(c) Null rigidity.** Let $\sigma:[0,1]\to C$ be future causal with
$\sigma(0)=p$, and let $\hat s\in(0,1]$ satisfy: $v(\sigma(\hat s))$ is
future null nonzero and $v(\sigma(t))\ne0$ for every $t\in(0,\hat s]$. Then
there are $v_0\in\mathcal N^+$ and a nondecreasing absolutely continuous
surjection $\varphi:[0,\hat s]\to[0,1]$ with
$\sigma(t)=\exp_p(\varphi(t)v_0)$ for $0\le t\le\hat s$.

**(d) Length maximality.** Let $\sigma:[0,1]\to C$ be future causal with
$\sigma(0)=p$. Then
$$L_g(\sigma)\le\sqrt{-D_p^2\bigl(\sigma(1)\bigr)}=\sqrt{-g_p\bigl(v(\sigma(1)),v(\sigma(1))\bigr)} .$$
If moreover $v(\sigma(1))$ is future timelike and $v(\sigma(t))\ne0$ for all
$t\in(0,1]$, then equality holds if and only if there are $v_0$ future
timelike and a nondecreasing absolutely continuous surjection
$\varphi:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ with $\sigma(t)=\exp_p(\varphi(t)v_0)$ for all $t$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]), let $p\in M$ and let $U_p=\exp_p(W_p)$
be a normal neighborhood of $p$ with $W_p$ star-shaped, as in
[[def-gr-normal-neighborhoods-and-position-vectors]] clause (a). Write
$v(q):=\exp_p^{-1}(q)$ for $q\in U_p$, $P(p,q):=d(\exp_p)_{v(q)}(v(q))$, and
$D_p^2(q):=g_p(v(q),v(q))$.

**(a) Differential in the second argument.** $D_p^2$ is smooth on $U_p$ and,
for every $q\in U_p$ and every $w\in T_qM$,
$$d(D_p^2)_q(w)=2\,g_q\bigl(P(p,q),w\bigr).$$

**(b) Reversal.** Let $q\in U_p$ and let $\gamma:[0,1]\to M$,
$\gamma(t)=\exp_p(t\,v(q))$, be the radial geodesic, so that
$\gamma(1)=q$. Then the reversed segment $t\mapsto\gamma(1-t)$ is the
restriction to $[0,1]$ of the maximal geodesic from $q$ with initial velocity
$-P(p,q)$; consequently
$$\exp_q^{-1}(p)=-P(p,q)\quad\text{and}\quad P(q,p)=-\,v(q)=-(\exp_p)^{-1}(q)$$
whenever the chosen normal inverse at $q$ has a domain containing
$-P(p,q)$. This condition holds in particular when both inverses are
those of one strictly convex normal set $C$ containing $p,q$ and the
inverse at $p$ used to define $v(q)$ is the one mapping $C$ to its
radial domain. Merely having $p,q\in C$ does not identify an independently
chosen inverse on $U_p$ with the inverse selected by $C$.
Under the inverse-domain condition, $D_q^2(p)=D_p^2(q)$ by the Gauss
lemma of [[thm-gr-lorentz-gauss-lemma-and-normal-maximum]].

**(c) Differential on pairs in a strictly convex normal set.** Use the inverse
domains selected by $C$ in this clause. If $C$ is a
strictly convex normal set ([[thm-gr-convex-normal-neighborhoods]]) and
$p,q\in C$, then

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]], [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]).
Call a map $x:I\to M$ a **geodesically connectible continuous causal curve**
when it is continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]) and for every strictly convex
normal ball $C$ as produced by [[thm-gr-convex-normal-neighborhoods]]
([[def-gr-normal-neighborhoods-and-position-vectors]] clause (b)) and all
$t_1<t_2$ in $I$ with $x([t_1,t_2])\subseteq C$, the endpoints $x(t_1)$ and

$C$. Write $\le$ for the causal relation of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] (defined by locally absolutely
continuous future causal curves) and put
$$n:=\frac{N}{\sqrt{-g(N,N)}},\qquad h:=g+2\,n^\flat\otimes n^\flat .$$

**(a) Absolutely continuous implies connectible.** Every future causal curve
$\gamma:I\to M$ in the sense of [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] is a
geodesically connectible continuous causal curve.

**(b) Connectible curves give causal relations.** Let $x:I\to M$ be a
geodesically connectible continuous causal curve and let $t_1<t_2$ in $I$.
If $x|_{[t_1,t_2]}$ is nonconstant, then for every open neighborhood $W$ of
$x([t_1,t_2])$ there is a piecewise smooth future causal curve
$\eta:[t_1,t_2]\to W$ with $\eta(t_1)=x(t_1)$ and $\eta(t_2)=x(t_2)$; in
particular $x(t_1)\le x(t_2)$. If the restriction is constant, its endpoints
coincide and reflexivity gives $x(t_1)\le x(t_2)$ without asserting a curve
in the nonconstant future causal class.

**(c) Equality of relations.** For $p,q\in M$ the following are equivalent:
$p\le q$; $p=q$ or there is a geodesically connectible continuous causal
curve with endpoints $p,q$.

**(d) One-sided extension.** Let $\gamma:[0,\infty)\to M$ be a
future-inextendible future causal curve in the sense of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] clause (d). Then there is an
inextendible future causal curve $\gamma^*:I^*\to M$ with
$[0,\infty)\subseteq I^*\subseteq\mathbb R$ and $\gamma^*|_{[0,\infty)}=\gamma$;
that is, $\gamma$ is contained in a curve that is both future- and
past-inextendible. The dual statement holds for past-inextendible curves.

No choice principle beyond the stated assumptions is used. The extension in (d) is not asserted to be
unique.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every open cover of a smooth manifold admits a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. If Omega has the specified finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, then $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F=\sum_j\int_{S_j}F\cdot\nu_j\,dS$, with faces counted once off E. All integrals are finite. In a specified finite gluing, the two fluxes on every shared face cancel.

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

derivations.claim: (Compact geometric regions.) For any compact $K$, $J^+(K)\cap\{t\le b\}$ is compact. Here is the needed argument, so volume time is not silently replaced by an arbitrary function in [F4]. First take $K=\{p\}$. The set is closed. If endpoints in it escape every auxiliary compact ball, joining causal curves from $p$ have unbounded auxiliary lengths. Their half-line limit from [F4] is future inextendible and has $t\le b$ everywhere, contradicting [F1]. Bounded lengths instead put the endpoints in a compact auxiliary ball. Thus the one-point truncation is compact. Cover a general compact $K$ by finitely many chronological futures $I^+(p_j)$ of points slightly to its past, as in the finite-cover proof of [F4]. Its future truncation is a closed subset of the finite union of the one-point truncations. Time reversal gives the past assertion. We also need compactness of $J^-(q)\cap J^+(\Sigma)$ for any Cauchy set $\Sigma$. This set is closed by its Cauchy sides and [F4]. If curves from $\Sigma$ to $q$ through an escaping sequence have unbounded lengths, parametrize backwards from $q$ and take a past-inextendible limit, all of whose points lie in the closed future side of $\Sigma$. Such a curve cannot meet $\Sigma$: its earlier nonconstant subarc would then lie in $\Sigma$, contrary to acausality. Its inextendible extension cannot meet $\Sigma$ to the future of $q$ either, again by acausality and the fact $q\in J^+(\Sigma)$. This contradicts the Cauchy property. Bounded lengths give compact auxiliary containment as before. The empty and singleton cases $q\in I^-(\Sigma)$ and $q\in\Sigma$ are immediate.

(Explicit first-order reduction.) In a splitting chart set $\rho=\alpha\sqrt{\det h}$, $H=(h^{ij})$, $v=\alpha^{-1}\partial_tu$ and $w_i=\partial_i u$. Direct expansion of $\Box_g$ gives
$$P u=\alpha^{-2}\partial_t^2u+b\partial_tu-h^{ij}\partial_i\partial_ju-c^j\partial_ju+Vu,\qquad b=\rho^{-1}\partial_t(\rho\alpha^{-2}),\quad c^j=\rho^{-1}\partial_i(\rho h^{ij}).$$
Solve instead the linear system for $U=(u,v,w_1,w_2,w_3)$ given by $u_t=\alpha v$, $(w_i)_t=\alpha\partial_iv+(\partial_i\alpha)v$, and
$$v_t=\alpha h^{ij}\partial_iw_j+\alpha c^jw_j-\alpha Vu-(\alpha_t/\alpha+\alpha^2b)v+\alpha f.$$
Multiplying the $w$ equations by $H$ gives symmetric principal matrices $A^0=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,H)$ and $(A^i)_{v,w_j}=(A^i)_{w_j,v}=-\alpha h^{ij}$, all other principal spatial entries zero. Thus $A^0>0$. A smooth solution of this system with initial $w_i=\partial_i u_0$ has $(w_i-\partial_iu)_t=0$, so these constraints remain zero, and the displayed expansion proves equivalence with $Pu=f$. Normal data initialize $v=u_1$. No sign of $V$ enters positivity of the principal matrices.

(Local solvability and a time independent of data size.) Restrict to a relatively compact splitting chart. Extend $A^0$ periodically by a smooth cutoff and interpolation with a constant positive matrix; convexity preserves positivity. Extend the other matrices and lower terms smoothly, agreeing on a smaller chart. To treat the source without an affine scaling error append the scalar $z$ with $z_t=0$, replace $f$ by $fz$, and initialize $z=1$. This is a homogeneous linear symmetric system in $(U,z)$, with coefficient family independent of its state and state domain all of $\mathbb R^6$. Apply [F2] at $s=5$ to the fixed class of data of $H^5$ norm at most one, with fixed compact admissible state balls containing their values by Sobolev embedding. An arbitrary smooth datum is multiplied by a positive constant making its norm at most one; after solving, divide by the same constant. Linearity restores the original datum and $z=1$. Consequently the local time depends on the coefficient extension and chart margins, not on the magnitude or higher norms of the datum. Smooth persistence applies on that same time. The coordinate finite-speed estimate of [F2] makes restrictions independent of the extension in smaller coordinate cones. This supplies local solutions and gluing uniqueness, but the sharper support assertion is proved next.

(Exact metric-cone energy.) Write the reduced system $A^\mu\partial_\mu U+CU=F$. Its current $j^\mu=U^{\mathsf T}A^\mu U$ obeys
$$\partial_\mu j^\mu=U^{\mathsf T}(\partial_\mu A^\mu-C-C^{\mathsf T})U+2U^{\mathsf T}F.$$
On compact charts, the right side is at most $C_0j^0+C_0|F|^2$. More precisely, for a covector $(\tau,\xi)$,
$$U^{\mathsf T}(\tau A^0+\xi_iA^i)U=\tau(u^2+v^2+h^{ij}w_iw_j)-2\alpha v h^{ij}\xi_iw_j\ge0\quad\text{if }\tau\ge\alpha\sqrt{h^{ij}\xi_i\xi_j}.$$
The inequality follows from Cauchy–Schwarz for $H$ and $2ab\le a^2+b^2$; its condition is exactly the future causal covector condition for $g=-\alpha^2dt^2+h$. In a sufficiently small convex normal chart, the boundary of the backward causal cone of a vertex has this outward null conormal, by [F3]. Truncate below the vertex and above a spacelike base, apply the coordinate divergence theorem, and discard the nonnegative lateral flux. Zero source and zero Cauchy data on the base give zero energy by Gronwall, hence zero solution up to the vertex by continuity. Every truncated cone away from its vertex is piecewise smooth: its null side is the smooth exponential null cone and its intersections with the temporal levels are transverse. No regularity of a global cut locus is asserted or used. This proves local dependence on the actual metric causal cone, rather than only a larger coordinate cone. Bounded lower-order terms, including arbitrary $V$ and its derivatives on each compact set, change $C_0$ and require no sign assumption.

(From local cones to global domain of dependence.) Fix a vertex $q$ to the future of the initial hypersurface and its compact truncated causal past from step 1.1. Cover it by finitely many smaller convex normal neighborhoods whose closures lie in coordinate neighborhoods as above. On this compact set the temporal derivative of a causal curve controls its coordinate speed: $h(\dot x,\dot x)\le\alpha^2\dot t^2$ and uniform upper/lower metric bounds give $|dx/dt|\le C$. Shrink a finite cover once more and choose $\delta>0$ smaller than its chart margins divided by $C+1$. Every backward causal segment of temporal duration below $\delta$ then lies in one of the larger normal neighborhoods. Local cones from step 2.2 therefore pass the zero-data assertion from one temporal cross-section of the truncated past to the next, in finitely many strips. At the initial surface use its local spacelike graph charts and the same cone flux with that graph as base; a finite cover of the compact shadow on the initial surface gives a uniform first strip. This proves zero at $q$ whenever the source vanishes on its truncated past and the initial data vanish on its shadow. Applying this to differences proves global uniqueness, even for smooth solutions with no support assumption, since only their values on a compact truncated past enter. Applying it outside the causal future of the source and data proves the claimed one-sided support; the source-free backward statement is its time reverse.

(Construction on a whole slice and continuation.) On a compact time slab let $Q$ be the union of the compact future and past support truncations of step 1.1 for the compact input supports. Around $Q$ fix a finite family of splitting coordinate cylinders, smaller cylinders, coefficient extensions and their margins. At an intermediate slice split the compact Cauchy data by a smooth finite partition subordinate to the smaller spatial charts; split the source in the same cylinders by a spacetime partition. For each summand initialize $u,v,w$ from that summand's scalar Cauchy data as in step 1.2. The local constructions of step 2.1 solve it on a common positive strip; finiteness takes the minimum of the times. Choose the strip shorter if needed so that the larger coordinate support cones from [F2] stay strictly inside their cylinders. Each summand then vanishes on a neighborhood of the lateral chart boundary and extends smoothly by zero; their finite sum solves the original scalar equation with the full data and source. Constraints for each summand were initialized from its own scalar datum, so no partition commutator error is introduced. Step 3.1 identifies this solution on overlaps and improves its support to the metric cones. The common strip width depends only on the fixed coefficient families, source and chart margins, not on current data size, by step 2.1. If continuation stopped at a finite end within the slab, start a strip less than half this fixed width before that end; uniqueness identifies its overlap and extends past the alleged end. Hence no such endpoint exists. Repeat over the countable slabs $[a-n,a+n]$ and use uniqueness to obtain one global smooth solution. Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $(M,g,N)$ and $P=-\Box_g+V$ have the smooth geometric and scalar-operator hypotheses of the Green-data definition, with arbitrary real $V\in C^\infty(M)$. No Green maps are assumed. Choose a smooth Cauchy temporal splitting $M=\mathbb R\times S$, $g=-\alpha^2dt^2+h_t$, with $\alpha>0$, and write $S_a=\{t=a\}$ and $\nu=\alpha^{-1}\partial_t$. For every $a\in\mathbb R$, $u_0,u_1\in C_c^\infty(S_a;\mathbb R)$ and $f\in C_c^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ there is a unique smooth solution

$$Pu=f,\qquad u|_{S_a}=u_0,\qquad \nu(u)|_{S_a}=u_1.$$

For $t\ge a$ its support is contained in $J^+(K_+)$, where $K_+=\operatorname{supp}u_0\cup\operatorname{supp}u_1\cup(\operatorname{supp}f\cap\{t\ge a\})$; the time-reversed assertion holds for $t\le a$. These are supports in the indicated closed half-spacetimes. On every finite time slab these support sets are compact. For fixed compact input supports, each compact-output derivative seminorm of $u$ is bounded by a constant times a finite sum of input derivative seminorms. For every Cauchy set $\Sigma$ and point $q$, the set $J^-(q)\cap J^+(\Sigma)$ and its time reverse are compact. Finally, on every smooth spacelike Cauchy hypersurface $\Sigma$, a smooth homogeneous solution with $u|_\Sigma=\nu(u)|_\Sigma=0$ vanishes identically, without a support hypothesis on that solution.

Let $M$ be a Hausdorff, second-countable smooth $n$-manifold without boundary. In a smooth chart $x=(x^1,\ldots,x^n)$, a smooth density is written $\phi_x(x)|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$. On a coordinate change $y=\psi(x)$ its coefficient transforms by
$$ \phi_y(y)=\phi_x(\psi^{-1}(y))\,|\det D\psi^{-1}(y)|. $$
A compactly supported smooth density is one whose support is compact in $M$. Give their space $\mathcal D(M;|\Lambda^nT^*M|)$ the locally convex test-density topology obtained from the usual fixed-compact derivative seminorms in charts and the corresponding LF inductive limit. A scalar distribution on $M$ is a continuous complex-linear functional on this test-density space, with bilinear pairing $\langle u,\omega\rangle$. Write $\mathcal D'(M)$ for these distributions and $\mathcal E'(M)$ for those with compact support. On a product manifold use the same definition with product densities. In a chart this definition is the ordinary distribution definition on an open subset of $\mathbb R^n$; the displayed Jacobian law is the coordinate compatibility condition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), as used to form the time-oriented Lorentzian geometric data below. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a Hausdorff, second-countable, oriented and time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold without boundary, with signature $(-,+,+,+)$, and assume it is globally hyperbolic in the convention of [[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]]: strongly causal and with compact causal diamonds. Curves and the causal sets $J^\pm(K)$ use the locally absolutely continuous causal-curve convention of [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]].

Write the positive metric density in a chart as $\mu_g=|\det(g_{ab})|^{1/2}|dx^0dx^1dx^2dx^3|$. This is a coordinate-independent smooth density: if $y=\psi(x)$, then $g_y=(D\psi^{-1})^Tg_xD\psi^{-1}$, so $|\det(g_y)|^{1/2}=|\det D\psi^{-1}|\,|\det(g_x)|^{1/2}$, the test-density transformation rule of [[def-qftx-distributions-on-smooth-manifolds]]. Let $\mathcal D_g(M):=C_c^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ have the real test-function topology transported by $f\mapsto f\mu_g$ from that supplier's compactly supported smooth test densities. Give $C^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ its usual topology of uniform convergence of every coordinate derivative on each compact subset.

For a real $V\in C^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ define the scalar Klein–Gordon-type operator $P=-\Box_g+V$, where $\Box_g f:=\mu_g^{-1}\partial_a(\mu_g g^{ab}\partial_b f)$ in a chart. Its principal symbol is $-g^{ab}\xi_a\xi_b$. No physical units are assigned; this is a mathematical differential operator. The Green-data interface below requires formal self-adjointness with respect to $\mu_g$, meaning $\int_M f(Pu)\,\mu_g=\int_M (Pf)u\,\mu_g$ for every $f\in\mathcal D_g(M)$ and $u\in C^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$; these integrals are finite because $P$ is local. The real solution space with spacelike-compact support is

$$\operatorname{Sol}_{\mathrm{sc}}(M):=\{u\in C^\infty(M;\mathbb R): Pu=0\text{ and }\operatorname{supp}u\subseteq J^+(K)\cup J^-(K)\text{ for some compact }K\subset M\}.$$

A **Green-data interface** for $(M,g,N,P)$ consists of continuous real-linear maps $E_+,E_-:\mathcal D_g(M)\to C^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$, called respectively retarded and advanced Green maps, such that for each $f\in\mathcal D_g(M)$,

$$PE_+f=E_+Pf=f,\qquad PE_-f=E_-Pf=f,$$

$$\operatorname{supp}(E_+f)\subseteq J^+(\operatorname{supp}f),\qquad \operatorname{supp}(E_-f)\subseteq J^-(\operatorname{supp}f).$$

The interface also includes uniqueness of the smooth Cauchy problem for $P$. For a smooth spacelike Cauchy hypersurface $\Sigma$ as defined in [[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]], let $\nu$ denote its unique future-directed unit timelike normal, characterized by orthogonality to $T\Sigma$, $g(\nu,\nu)=-1$ and $g(\nu,N)<0$; the Cauchy data of a smooth $u$ are $u|_\Sigma$ and the normal derivative $\nu(u)|_\Sigma$. The uniqueness condition is that a smooth solution of $Pu=0$ with both data zero on $\Sigma$ is zero.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every open cover of a smooth manifold admits a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

derivations.claim: (Retarded construction.) Fix the smooth time $t$ of [F1]. For nonzero compact test $f$, choose $a<\min t(\operatorname{supp}f)$ and solve $Pu=f$ with zero data on $S_a$ using [F1]. Below that slice the source and both data vanish, so uniqueness and its time-reversed support assertion give $u=0$. Above it the one-sided support assertion gives $\operatorname{supp}u\subseteq J^+(\operatorname{supp}f)$. Define $E_+f=u$ and $E_+0=0$. A different sufficiently early slice gives the same solution: both solutions have zero data on a still earlier common slice and the same source, so [F1] uniqueness identifies them. Reversing time constructs $E_-f$ from zero data on any slice later than the support and gives the past support.

(Two-sided inverse identities and uniqueness.) The construction gives $PE_\pm f=f$. If $k$ is compact, locality gives $\operatorname{supp}Pk\subseteq\operatorname{supp}k$. The compact smooth function $k$ and $E_+(Pk)$ both solve $Pu=Pk$ and have zero data on a common slice earlier than $\operatorname{supp}k$; uniqueness gives $E_+Pk=k$. The advanced identity is time reversed. If any other smooth retarded solution of $Pu=f$ has support in $J^+(\operatorname{supp}f)$, it has zero data on that earlier slice and equals $E_+f$ by [F1]. The same holds for advanced solutions, proving uniqueness of the maps. Common early or late slices for a finite list of tests and uniqueness give additivity and real homogeneity, hence real linearity.

(Continuity in the actual topologies.) Fix compact input support $K$ and compact output set $L$ with a specified derivative order. Choose $a<\min t(K)$ and a finite slab containing $S_a$ and $L$; if $K$ is empty the restriction is zero. Step 1.1 constructs every $E_+f$ for $\operatorname{supp}f\subseteq K$ from zero data on this same $S_a$. The estimate in [F1] therefore bounds the selected output seminorm by a constant times finitely many fixed-$K$ input derivative seminorms. This proves continuity of $E_+$ restricted to each fixed-compact test space. The LF topology in [F2] is the locally convex inductive-limit topology of these spaces, so a linear map into the locally convex space $C^\infty(M)$ is continuous precisely when all such restrictions are continuous. Thus $E_+$ is continuous; the late-slice estimate gives continuity of $E_-$. No sequential-continuity substitute or unsupported closed-graph argument is used.

(The remaining interface conditions.) For compact smooth $f$ and arbitrary smooth $u$, the coordinate divergence expression for $\Box_g$ and integration by parts give
$$\int_M f(-\Box_g u)\,\mu_g=\int_M g^{ab}(\partial_af)(\partial_bu)\,\mu_g=\int_M(-\Box_g f)u\,\mu_g.$$
These identities are justified by localizing the compact support to finitely many charts using [F2]: the extra partition derivatives sum to zero, and each chart integration has compact support. Multiplication by the real $V$ is symmetric, proving formal self-adjointness. Arbitrary smooth spacelike Cauchy-surface uniqueness is the last conclusion of [F1]. Together with steps 1.1–3.1 these establish every condition in the defined Green-data interface for the full stated class of backgrounds.
